The Two Lives of Q, K, and V: How the Same Vectors Build the Substrate and Then Read from It

Ben Um • April 13, 2026

In the previous chapter, we introduced the triad — Q, K, and V — and described how they collaborate during decode to reconstruct implicit sense from across the substrate. But we described only half of their lives. The same three vectors play a fundamentally different role during prefill, and understanding this difference is essential to understanding why prompts have permanent consequences.

The Same Letters, Two Different Jobs

Every explanation of Q, K, and V describes the same mechanism: Q asks a question, K advertises relevance, V delivers content. The dot product between Q and K produces attention weights, and those weights select a blend of V vectors. This is correct. But it leaves out something critical: when this mechanism fires determines what it does.

During decode, the mechanism serves two purposes simultaneously. First, it is a retrieval operation: a newly generated token produces a Q vector that searches the existing substrate, matching against cached K vectors to select which cached V vectors deliver their content. Second, it is an extension operation: that same token’s own K and V vectors — shaped by what Q gathered — are appended to the substrate, becoming part of the context that all future tokens will read from. The substrate grows with every generated token.

During prefill, the mechanism is a construction operation. Every token in the prompt has its K and V vectors built and frozen into the substrate in a single pass. The critical difference is not that prefill writes and decode reads — both phases write K and V vectors into the substrate. The difference is who controls what gets written. During prefill, the prompt author controls the input entirely. During decode, the model controls what gets generated, and each generated token’s K and V are shaped by the model’s own choices. The prompt author’s influence over the substrate is concentrated in prefill. After that, the model takes over.

The linear algebra is identical in both phases. The authorship is not.

Prefill: Q as Builder

To see what this means concretely, return to the sentence from the earlier chapters.

“A dry log crackled and split as the campfire grew.”

When the transformer processes this sentence during prefill, it moves through the tokens in order, computing K and V vectors at each position. At each position, the token’s Q vector reaches back to attend to everything that came before it.

When the transformer reaches “log,” Q at that position attends to “A” and “dry.” The attention mechanism computes how relevant those preceding tokens are to “log” and pulls information from their V vectors into the residual stream. This enriched residual stream is then projected through the K and V weight matrices, producing the K and V vectors that are frozen at the “log” position.

This is where Q’s role as builder becomes visible. The K vector at “log” does not simply encode the token ID for “log.” It encodes “log as preceded by ‘a dry,’” and all the associations that attention extracted from those preceding tokens. Q was the mechanism that performed that extraction. Q asked the question: what do the tokens before me carry that is relevant to what I am? The answer to that question shaped the K and V vectors that were written at this position.

If Q had failed to attend to “dry” — if the attention weights had distributed poorly at some layer — the K and V vectors at the “log” position would be correspondingly impoverished. They would carry less information about desiccated timber, less enrichment from the preceding context. And this impoverishment would be permanent. No future token can reach back and rewrite what was frozen here.

This is the fundamental asymmetry. During prefill, Q has irreversible consequences. The quality of attention at each layer, at each position, permanently determines what gets written into the substrate. Every K and V vector in the cache is a record of how well Q did its job at that position during prefill.

Decode: Q as Reader and Extender

During decode, Q operates in a different context. The substrate built during prefill already exists — every K and V vector from the prompt is frozen in the cache. The model is now generating tokens one at a time, and each new token produces a Q vector that searches the entire substrate.

Consider what happens when the model is generating a response about the campfire scene. The current token’s Q vector expresses what the model needs right now — perhaps information about the physical setting, the quality of the fire, the state of the fuel. That Q vector is compared against every K vector in the cached substrate. Positions whose K vectors advertise relevant content — the position where “log” sits, the position where “crackled” sits — receive high attention weights. Their corresponding V vectors deliver content into the blend.

If the Q vector at this decode step is poorly formed — if it fails to express the right question — the model may attend to the wrong positions and produce a weak prediction. The K and V vectors at existing positions are not corrupted by this failure. They remain exactly as they were. The next decode step generates a fresh Q vector and gets another chance to read the substrate well.

But the consequences of a bad decode step are not entirely local. Each generated token also writes its own K and V vectors into the substrate. Those vectors are shaped by what Q gathered during that token’s forward pass. If Q attended poorly, the K and V vectors appended at that position will be correspondingly weak — and every future token will read from a substrate that now contains that weakness. The error does not corrupt what came before, but it does extend the substrate with impoverished content that all subsequent tokens must work with.

Compare this with prefill. During prefill, Q’s failures are embedded in the foundation — the substrate that the entire generation will read from. During decode, Q’s failures are embedded in the extension — the growing portion of the substrate that later generated tokens will read from. Both are permanent. But the prefill substrate is shaped by the prompt author. The decode extension is shaped by the model. This is why the quality of the prompt has outsized influence: it determines the foundation on which every generated token builds.

The Residual Stream: Where Construction Happens

To understand why prefill Q has permanent consequences, it helps to see where in the computation the writing actually happens. This requires understanding what a forward pass is.

A forward pass is one complete traversal through every layer of the transformer, from input embeddings to final output. During prefill, there is one forward pass that processes all prompt tokens through every layer. During decode, there is one forward pass per generated token. A model with 80 layers means 80 sequential steps — layer 1 must complete before layer 2 can begin, because each layer’s input is the previous layer’s output.

At each layer during this forward pass, every token has a residual stream — a running representation that accumulates information as it passes through the transformer’s layers. At each attention layer, the Q vector for the current token attends to preceding positions, pulls a weighted blend of V vectors, and adds the result back into the residual stream. Then the residual stream passes through the layer’s feedforward network, which further transforms it. This updated residual stream becomes the input to the next layer.

At every layer, the residual stream is projected through the K and V weight matrices for that layer to produce the K and V vectors that are stored in the cache. This means the K and V vectors at a given position are not computed once from the raw embedding. They are computed at every layer, each time from a residual stream that has been progressively enriched by all the attention and feedforward operations in the layers before it.

This has a structural implication worth making explicit: the KV substrate is not a flat surface. A model with 80 layers stores 80 K vectors and 80 V vectors at every token position — 160 vectors per position, each capturing a different level of abstraction. Shallow layers hold surface-level patterns. Deep layers hold abstract semantic relationships. During decode, Q at each layer reads exclusively from that same layer’s cached K and V vectors. Layer 12’s decode Q reads from layer 12’s cached K and V. Layer 60’s decode Q reads from layer 60’s cached K and V. The layers never cross. The substrate has depth as well as width — it is a lattice, not a ledger.

Q’s role in this process is cumulative. At layer 1, Q pulls basic information from preceding tokens. At layer 2, Q operates on a residual stream that already contains the information pulled at layer 1, and pulls additional, potentially more abstract information. By layer 30 or 50 or 80, the residual stream at a given position has been shaped by dozens of rounds of Q-driven attention, each building on the last. The K and V vectors stored at the final layer reflect the full depth of this progressive enrichment.

This is why Q during prefill is a builder. It does not just read information — it gathers and folds information into the residual stream, and the residual stream is the raw material from which K and V vectors are made. The same is true during decode: each generated token’s Q gathers from the existing substrate, and the result shapes the K and V vectors that are appended. The difference is that during prefill, Q is building the foundation. During decode, Q is extending it.

K Shifts Between Phases

Q’s role shift is the most dramatic, but K also changes character between the two phases.

During prefill, K plays a dual role. At each position, K is being written — projected from the residual stream and stored in the cache. But K vectors at earlier positions are simultaneously being read by later tokens within the same prefill pass. When token 5’s Q computes attention at layer 3, it matches against the K vectors at positions 0 through 5 — K vectors that were just computed in the same parallel operation. K during prefill is both product and advertisement: newly manufactured and immediately serving its matchmaking function for every token that follows.

During decode, K’s role narrows. The cached K vectors from prefill are now static — they sit in the cache and cannot update themselves, cannot respond to what Q is looking for, cannot improve their advertisement based on what the model now needs. They are frozen exactly as they were written. New K vectors are added at each decode step for the generated tokens, but the K vectors from the prompt positions are permanent.

This is another way to see why prefill quality matters. The K vectors from the prompt form the core of the substrate that decode Q searches against. If prefill Q did its job well — pulling rich context from preceding tokens into the residual stream — then those K vectors accurately advertise what each position carries. Decode Q can search effectively because the advertisements are good. If prefill Q did its job poorly, those K vectors are vague or misleading, and decode Q must work harder to find what it needs — or may fail to find it at all.

V Shifts in the Same Way

V follows the same pattern as K. During prefill, V plays a dual role: V vectors are being written to the cache at each position, while V vectors at earlier positions are being read from by later tokens’ attention within the same pass. When Q at the “log” position attends to “dry,” it reads the V vector at the “dry” position and folds that content into the residual stream. V during prefill is simultaneously payload being manufactured and payload being delivered.

During decode, V’s role narrows to delivery. The cached V vectors are read from whenever the Q·K matchmaking selects them. New V vectors are appended for generated tokens, but the V vectors from the prompt positions are frozen.

This is the machinery behind the enrichment described in the previous chapter. When we said that the explicit sense at “log” is enriched by “a dry” — that enrichment happened because Q at the “log” position read V vectors from the “a” and “dry” positions and folded their content into the residual stream, which was then projected into the K and V vectors frozen at “log.”

Why Q Is Not in the Cache

If Q, K, and V are all computed at every position, a natural question arises: why is it called the KV cache and not the QKV cache?

K and V are position-bound. They encode what a specific token carries at a specific position in the sequence, shaped by everything that preceded it. That information is needed by every future token that attends to that position. It has to persist.

Q is moment-bound. It expresses what one token needs at one layer during one step of the forward pass. Once that Q has attended to the K vectors, selected the relevant V vectors, and folded the result into the residual stream, its job is done. No future token will ever need to know what token 5 was looking for at layer 12. The question was asked, the answer was gathered, and the residual stream moved on. Q is discarded.

This is true in both phases. During decode, each new token generates a Q vector, reads the substrate, and the Q is gone. During prefill, every token’s Q at every layer is equally ephemeral — used once for gathering and then discarded. The difference is that Q’s work is immortalized in the K and V vectors that are frozen from the residual stream it helped shape. Q does not survive the forward pass. But the K and V vectors it made possible do.

The builder does not live in the building. Only the building remains.

Why This Distinction Matters

The practical consequence of this dual role is stark: the substrate that the prompt author controls is written entirely during prefill, and once written, it cannot be revised.

When you write a prompt, you are not just providing input. You are providing the raw material for a construction process. Every token in your prompt will have its K and V vectors built by the prefill attention mechanism — Q gathering from preceding context, the residual stream accumulating, K and V being projected and frozen. The quality of what you write determines the quality of what gets built. The order of your tokens determines what context is available when each position’s K and V vectors are computed.

Once prefill is complete, the foundation is set. The model will read from it for the entire duration of generation, and every generated token will extend the substrate further. But that extension is built on top of the foundation the prompt established. The generated tokens attend to the prompt’s K and V vectors, gather from them, and build their own representations on what they find there. A strong foundation produces strong extensions. A weak foundation forces the model to build on impoverished ground.

This is why front-loading context matters — not as a prompt engineering trick, but as a mechanical necessity. Placing disambiguating context before the tokens that need it ensures that prefill Q has the right material to work with when building K and V vectors at those positions. Placing it after means the K and V vectors are already frozen in an impoverished state, and the model must rely on implicit sense — the more expensive, more distributed, less concentrated reconstruction process — to recover what was never written in the first place.

The research community has begun to discover this asymmetry empirically, even without naming it conceptually. Recent work on KV cache compression has found that evaluating token importance using prefill-phase attention patterns produces systematically different results than evaluating importance from decode-phase patterns. The tokens that prefill Q attended to most heavily are not necessarily the tokens that decode Q will need most. This makes sense once the two phases are seen clearly: prefill Q was building the foundation, optimizing for construction. Decode Q is reading the foundation and extending the substrate, optimizing for retrieval and generation. They are doing different jobs, and the tokens they prioritize reflect those different purposes.

In the next chapter, we will see the full consequence of these mechanics in practice. When external knowledge is injected into a prompt through retrieval — a technique known as RAG — every token in that injected content passes through prefill. The framing that surrounds it, the order in which it appears, the context that precedes it — all of this shapes the K and V vectors that are frozen for every token in the retrieved passage. The substrate is not a neutral container. It is a construction, and the architect is the prompt.
